newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine economic data show surprising strength.
newsitem.headline: Argentine economic data show surprising strength.

text.p: The Argentine economy, mired in deep recession one year ago, showed surprising strength in the fourth quarter of 1996, with industrial production heading for record levels, according to data released by the government on Thursday.
The Economy Ministry said gross domestic product, the total value of the nation's output of goods and services, grew 4.4 percent in 1996 after shrinking by 4.6 percent in 1995.
The data indicated that most of the growth in Argentina, a major exporter of grains, came in the fourth quarter when output climbed 9.2 percent.
They were heartening numbers for the government of President Carlos Menem, whose Peronist Party trails in the polls ahead of October legislative elections.
"The 1996 result surprised us analysts as much as it did the government," said Osvaldo Cortesi, chief economist with the consulting and forecasting firm Macroeconomica.
The growth figure was testimony to an economic surge since 1995 when Argentina was plunged into recession by Mexico's financial crisis.
The government had anticipated growth of only three percent last year, and private analysts were no more optimistic.
"We have recovered a great part of the fall registered in 1995," a ministry report said.
Separately, Industry Secretary Alieto Guadagni forecast Argentine industrial output would grow this year by more than five percent to reach a record high.

Guadagni highlighted the sector's performance between 1990 and 1996. In that period, output grew at a yearly average of 4.5 percent, versus an average drop of two percent a year between 1981 and 1990.
Economists said much of the 1996 GDP growth reflected a late-year boom in exports to Brazil, Argentina's largest trading partner, and other fellow members of the Mercosur customs union.
The robust gain also came on the heels of a recovery in consumer spending that exceeded all expectations.
To be sure, the government, which forecasts five percent economic growth this year, is more anxious about a reduction in the jobless rate by three or four percentage points before October elections.

The Peronists hold a slim minority in the lower house of Congress, where half of the seats will be contested in the autumn. Voters and analysts say the country's biggest problem is unemployment, now at 17.3 percent.
Since he first came to power in 1989, Menem has had more success in driving down inflation, which was reduced from 5,000 percent to zero last year.
